title: Case Studies and Challenges in Reproducibility in the Computational Sciences
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of reproducibility in computational science research and the practical barriers that prevent others from rerunning, verifying, or extending published work. The authors frame reproducibility as a cornerstone of scientific method and argue that, in computational fields, reproducibility depends not only on code and data but also on ethics procedures, software environments, licensing, and dissemination practices.

The paper is organized around four case studies. First, it analyzes ethics requirements across ten universities to identify a minimum set of ethical metadata that should accompany studies involving human subjects. Second, it tests whether parallel and distributed experiments can be recomputed reliably in virtualized/cloud environments, using a parallel maximum-clique implementation and a Chord distributed hash table deployment. Third, it packages three non-computer-science computational experiments (urban planning, solar physics, and atmospheric physics) into VMs and examines legal and technical obstacles to recomputation. Fourth, it studies the recomputability of an HCI experiment by asking multiple groups to reproduce the statistical analysis of previously collected data.

Across these cases, the authors conclude that reproducibility is feasible in some settings, especially for sequential or well-contained computational workflows, but is often constrained by inconsistent ethics requirements, legal/IP restrictions, proprietary dependencies, tool usability issues, and differences in background knowledge. They recommend sharing data, code, scripts, and methodological metadata, and argue for stronger cultural and tooling support to make recomputation routine.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/reproducibility case-study paper, not a peer-reviewed causal study of an educational intervention. It contains some empirical observations, but they are small-scale, descriptive, and not designed to estimate effects on learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct K-12 learning intervention or student outcome impact. Its contribution is indirect, focused on research reproducibility, ethics metadata, and workflow challenges rather than educational effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a reproducibility and research-process study, not a student-outcome intervention study. It reports substantial institutional variability in ethics review requirements across 10 universities, with 145 unique attributes identified and only 2 fields common to all forms (principal investigator name and whether informed consent was sought). The practical impact is mixed: the authors derive a proposed 15-attribute minimum ethics specification, but the study does not evaluate educational outcomes.
finding.measure: Comparative content analysis of institutional ethics application forms

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that recomputation workflows can be feasible but remain cumbersome, especially for multi-machine and cross-tool analyses. In the HCI recomputation exercise, teams spent about 90 minutes and only achieved partial verification; one group could verify an ANOVA result, while others only reproduced descriptive statistics, reflecting substantial overhead from tool, data, and script issues.
finding.measure: Success in recomputing published analyses; time and obstacles required to reproduce statistics
